title: Chevron stripe lap throw
subtitle: A 100 by 120 cm lap throw in a yarn-over chevron pattern, two colours, DK.
excerpt: A 100 by 120 cm lap throw worked flat in a simple yarn-over chevron with two colours alternating every two rows. The chevron uses k2tog and yarn-over to create the zigzag. About 400 g of DK in two colours.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, 7th series (1891), §Ripple Knitting, documents a two-colour chevron in DK weight as a drawing-room throw pattern. The yarn-over chevron construction is also described in Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), §Chevron Patterns.

knitting.gaugeText: 22 sts × 30 rows = 10 × 10 cm in chevron pattern on 4 mm needles, unblocked.

glossaryTerms.definition: Wrapping the working yarn over the right needle between two stitches without knitting a stitch. Creates an extra stitch and a small hole. Used in lace and chevron patterns to compensate for a decrease elsewhere in the same row, keeping the stitch count constant.
Inserting the right needle through two stitches at once and knitting them as a single stitch, creating a right-slanting decrease that reduces the stitch count by one.

content.text: A single-panel rectangle worked flat on 4 mm needles. The pattern uses a two-colour chevron:
decreases. Finished size: 100 cm wide by 120 cm long.

Single-panel construction, no seams. The chevron was chosen because the yarn-over-and-decrease pattern produces a reversible zigzag fabric with no curling, which means no border treatment is needed. Two colours are carried up the side and changed every two rows, producing fine horizontal stripes within the chevron silhouette. At DK weight the drape is lighter than chunky chevron alternatives. Budget about 400 g of each colour (about 880 m / 960 yards per colour). Buy yarn in matched dye lots.

items.qty: 400 g (about 880 m / 960 yards) of DK-weight yarn

content.text: 22 stitches and 30 rows to 10 cm in chevron pattern on 4 mm needles. The chevron pattern produces a slightly shorter row gauge than stocking stitch (more rows per 10 cm). Swatch the full 10-stitch repeat for at least 10 cm before casting on.
If your row gauge is 28 rows per 10 cm, the same row count produces the throw about 4 cm longer. Measure by tape to the target 120 cm rather than by row count.

Using Yarn A and the long-tail cast-on, cast on 220 stitches (a multiple of 10, plus 2 edge stitches; the chevron repeat is 10 stitches wide). Long-tail tail: (4 × 220) / 10 + 15 = 88 + 15 = 103 cm. Measure 120 cm.
RS rows: k1, *k2tog, k3, yo, k4; rep from * to last st, k1.

Colour sequence: work 2 rows Yarn A, then 2 rows Yarn B, carrying the unused yarn up the left edge. Continue alternating until the throw measures 120 cm. When you set this aside, note which colour is on the needle and whether the next row is a RS or WS row.

At row 180 (about 60 cm): count across. You should have 220 stitches. Each k2tog decrease pairs with a yo increase so the total count stays constant throughout. At row 358 (about 119 cm): count again before casting off.
Stitch count drifting: a yo was placed without a matching k2tog in the same row, or vice versa. Count stitches at the end of each RS row during the first repeat until the pattern is automatic.

Chevron peaks misaligning between RS rows: a WS row was worked as a RS row (with the k2tog and yo). All WS rows in this pattern are plain knit; if the chevron is the same on both sides of the work, the WS row was worked as RS by mistake.
Cast off knitwise with a relaxed tension, using whichever colour is active at 120 cm.
Weave in all yarn-change ends along the side edge. A light wet block will sharpen the chevron points.
Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle for superwash DK. Lay flat to dry.

From a two-colour chevron, try feather-and-fan next. The yarn-over and decrease technique is the same. The spacing changes: more decreases cluster together. The result is a scalloped edge instead of a pointed chevron.
